newsitem.title: USA: Simpson verdict grabs U.S. attention.
newsitem.headline: Simpson verdict grabs U.S. attention.

text.p: The verdict against O. J. Simpson was the talk of the town across the United States on Wednesday, with evidence of nagging racial division over the case and some exasperation at the way it has dominated the news for two and a half years.
The saga's latest chapter nearly pushed President Bill Clinton off the front pages of some newspapers.

In Chicago, WGN-TV said its live coverage from the Santa Monica courthouse on Tuesday night drew the highest audience share in the country's third largest city when most other stations were carrying Clinton's State of the Union speech.

An ABC-TV poll found that 66 percent of Americans agreed with the verdict blaming Simpson for the deaths of his ex-wife and her friend, but with significant divisions between blacks and whites. A CBS poll found 68 percent backed the verdict.
An America On Line chat room devoted to the case was jammed with electronic gossips and the service reported a huge increase in traffic on computer newsgroups after the verdict.
In Boston, legal clerk Robin Cabral said she thought "the media just made too much of this whole thing. It was ridiculous." But she added: "I was convinced from Day One that he was guilty."
Lenny Carlson, an accounting manager for a mutual fund in Boston, also called the media focus on Simpson since the murders of ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson and her friend Ronald Goldman "excessive."

"They raised enough doubt in the (1995) criminal case as to whether or not he did it, but in the civil trial, when he took the stand and testified, he did himself in," Carlson said. "He wound up just saying everybody else was lying. I mean those photos with the shoes and limousine driver."

But Frank Creft in Charlotte, North Carolina, disagreed. "As an African American attorney I am not surprised about the verdict," he said. "Most of the African American community realised that when the trial was in Santa Monica that it was destined that he would be found liable because it was obvious after the murder trial that white America was upset about the verdict and this was an opportunity to point the finger at him to say, 'He did it.'

"What troubles me is the reaction of the white American community. When the decision was televised they reacted the same way as African Americans did to the verdict in the criminal trial and (blacks) were criticised."

There were cheers outside the courthouse when the mainly white jury ruled against Simpson and awarded Goldman's family $8.5 million in damages. Some TV footage from nightspots showed white patrons hailing the verdict much as blacks were seen celebrating Simposon's acquittal 16 months earlier.

Radio talk shows crackled with commentary. At WSB-AM in Atlanta one caller said: "I think Simpson has gotten what he deserves. At the very least, he will have to live in shame. He'll have to face his children every day."
